column2: Price reacts to the surprise, meaning the difference between the actual figure and the forecast, not to the figure itself. A good but already expected number may barely move the price, while an unexpected one can trigger a big move, in either direction. Nobody knows the direction in advance, so don't try to guess it.
Risk management
How to protect yourself
The rules I follow around the news. They are risk management rules, not trading recommendations.
Check the week on Sunday and the day each morning
On Sunday I look at which big releases are coming in the week ahead, and each morning I check that day. Write down the times of the high-impact news for the pairs you follow.
No new trades 15–30 minutes before and after
Around a high-impact release, I don't open new positions. I let the market calm down and only then look at the chart again.
Spreads widen and slippage appears
Just before and right after the announcement, liquidity drops. The spread can widen several times over, and orders can fill at a different price than the one you asked for.
Your stop loss can be filled at a worse price
If the price jumps past your level, your stop loss closes at the first available price. The loss can be bigger than you planned, even if you did everything right.
Reduce your lot or stay out
If you do trade on a day with big news, use a smaller risk and recalculate your lot in the calculator. Not trading at all is also a good decision.
Swing trading: watch the positions you hold through the news
If you hold a position for several days, check which big releases are coming before your target. Decide in advance, in your plan, whether you keep it, reduce your risk or close it.
Remember
You check the calendar before every trading day and know the times of the big releases.

A dictionary for beginners
Forex glossary: terms explained simply
60 terms you'll come across early on, briefly explained, with links to the beginner course and the tools on the site.
Search the glossary
60 terms
Backtest
Testing a strategy on past data to see how it would have performed. Past results don't guarantee future results, but they help you see whether your rules make sense.
Central bank
The institution that sets the policy interest rate for a currency, for example the Fed (US) or the ECB (euro area). Central bank decisions and speeches are among the most important events for Forex.
Bearish
Pessimistic, expecting the price to fall. A bearish market generally makes lower highs and lower lows. A bearish candle closes below its open.
Bid and ask
The bid is the price at which you can sell, the ask the price at which you can buy (always slightly higher). You buy at the ask and sell at the bid, and the difference between them is the spread.
Break-even

The point where you neither win nor lose. "Moving your SL to break-even" means moving it to your entry price. The break-even win rate is the minimum percentage of winning trades you need to come out even: 1 ÷ (1 + R).
Breakout
The price leaving a zone or pattern, for example above a resistance or out of a triangle. Many breakouts are false, which is why many traders wait for the candle to close or for a retest.
The company that gives you access to the market: you open an account, deposit money and trade on a platform. Always check the regulation, the costs and how easily you can withdraw your money.
Bullish
Optimistic, expecting the price to rise. A bullish market generally makes higher highs and higher lows. A bullish candle closes above its open.

Contract for difference: an instrument that tracks the price of an asset without you owning it. You win or lose the price difference, with leverage. At brokers for retail clients, Forex is usually traded through CFDs. See chapter 1.
Commission
A fixed fee per lot, charged by some account types instead of a wider spread. When you compare brokers, compare the total cost: spread, commission and swap.
Demo account
An account with virtual money and real prices, offered for free by brokers. It's where you learn the platform and test your plan without risk, with the same rules you'd use live. See chapter 8.

The consumer price index, the main measure of inflation. Inflation above expectations can change the central bank's interest rate plans and move the currency strongly. The data appears in the economic calendar.
Day trading
A style where you open and close positions on the same day, without holding them overnight. It takes a lot of screen time and quick decisions.
Drawdown
How far the account has fallen from its highest point, usually in percent. Big losses are hard to recover: after −50% you need +100% to get back. See chapter 6.
ECN and market maker

An ECN broker passes your orders to liquidity providers, usually with a tight spread plus commission. A market maker is itself the counterparty to your trades. Both models can be fair, as long as the broker is regulated.
Equity
Your account balance plus or minus the profit or loss of positions that are still open. Margin and stop out are calculated from equity, not from balance.

The European Securities and Markets Authority. Its CFD rules protect retail clients in the EU: maximum leverage of 1:30 on major pairs, positions closed out at 50% of margin and negative balance protection. See chapter 4.
The Fear Of Missing Out on a move: you jump into a trade late, without a logical stop loss. A missed entry is not a loss. See chapter 7.
Gap

A jump in price over a range where no trading happened, usually between Friday's close and Monday's open or on major news. A gap can skip past your stop loss, and the exit happens at the first available price.
Trading journal
Your notes on every trade: the pair, the reason for entering, SL, TP, the result in R and whether you followed your plan. You can use the journal on this site for free.
Leverage

It lets you open a position much larger than the money in your account: at 1:30, every €1 in your account controls €30. Profit and loss are calculated on the whole position, so leverage magnifies losses just as much. See chapter 4.
Liquidity
How easily you can buy or sell without moving the price. High liquidity means tight spreads and good execution; it's usually highest during the London and New York session overlap.
Long and short
Long (buy) means you expect the price to rise, short (sell) that you expect it to fall. In Forex you can trade both directions just as easily.

The unit for position size. 1 standard lot = 100,000 units of the base currency, 0.10 lots = 10,000, and 0.01 lots (micro) = 1,000. You can work out how many lots to open with the lot size calculator.
Candlestick
A way of showing price over a period: the open, close, high and low. Green if it closed above the open, red if below. See chapter 2.
Risk management
The rules that protect your account: a maximum of 1% risk per trade, always a stop loss, a lot sized by risk and daily and weekly loss limits. See chapter 6 and the basic rules.
Margin call
The broker's warning that your free margin has run out and the account is getting close to a forced close of positions. The exact level is set by the broker.
Margin
The part of your account the broker locks up as collateral for an open position: margin = position value ÷ leverage. It isn't a cost, it's money set aside while the position is open. See chapter 4.

The monthly report on jobs created in the US outside agriculture, usually published on the first Friday of the month at 8:30 New York time. It's one of the releases that moves the market the most. You'll find it in the economic calendar.
Limit order
A pending order at a better price than the current one: buy limit below the price, sell limit above it. You use it when you're waiting for a pullback.
Market order
You enter immediately, at the current available price. It's the simplest type of order. See chapter 5.
Stop order
A pending order that triggers when the price confirms the direction: buy stop above the current price, sell stop below it. It's often used for breakouts.
Overtrading
Too many trades, out of boredom or the urge to win back losses. The antidote: only enter the setups in your plan. See chapter 7.
Exotic pair
A major currency paired with the currency of a smaller or emerging economy, for example USDTRY or EURPLN. The spread is wider and moves can be abrupt. When you're starting out, stick to the majors.
Major pair
A pair made up of the US dollar and one of the other big currencies: EURUSD, GBPUSD, USDJPY, USDCHF, AUDUSD, USDCAD, NZDUSD. They have high liquidity and usually the lowest costs.
Minor pair (cross)
A pair of major currencies without the US dollar, for example EURGBP, EURJPY or GBPJPY. Costs are usually slightly higher than on the majors.
Pip
The smallest "standard" price move of a currency pair. On most pairs, 1 pip = 0.0001 (the fourth decimal); on yen (JPY) pairs, 1 pip = 0.01. Details in chapter 3 of the course.
Negative balance protection
The rule that, at EU brokers, a retail client can't lose more than the money in their account. Brokers outside the EU aren't required to apply it.
Point (pipette)
One decimal place beyond the pip: 10 points = 1 pip. Platforms such as MetaTrader show prices with 5 decimals (3 on JPY pairs), and distances often appear in points rather than pips.
Risk/reward ratio (R:R)

Compares how much you risk with how much you can make: a 25-pip SL and a 50-pip TP means 1:2. At 1:2 you need at least 33.3% winning trades to break even, before costs. You can work it out with the risk/reward calculator.
Retest
The price coming back to the level it has just broken before continuing in the direction of the breakout. For example, a broken resistance gets tested from above, as support.
Revenge trading
After a loss you want to "win it back" right away, usually with a bigger lot. The antidote: after 2 losses in a row, close the platform until the next day. See chapter 7.
Resistance
A price zone where rallies have stalled several times, because sellers showed up there. Broken support can become resistance, and vice versa.
Scalping
A very fast style, with trades lasting seconds or minutes on small timeframes. Costs (spread, commission) weigh heavily, and for a beginner it's the hardest style.
Trading session
The hours when a major financial centre is active: Sydney, Tokyo, London, New York. On the Sessions page you can see live which sessions are open, in your time.
Slippage
The difference between the price you asked for and the price your order was filled at. It mostly happens around news or when the market moves very fast, and it can work for or against you.
Balance
The money in your account excluding open positions: deposits, plus or minus the result of trades already closed. It only changes when you close a position.
Spread
The difference between the buy price (ask) and the sell price (bid). It's the main cost of a trade and it widens around news, at night and when the market reopens. See chapter 1.
Stop loss (SL)
The order that automatically closes your position at a loss at a price you set in advance. You place it where your idea is proven wrong and never move it further away. See chapter 5.
Stop out

The level at which the broker automatically closes your positions, because equity has fallen too far relative to the margin used. In the EU, for retail clients, positions are closed when equity falls below 50% of the initial margin required.
Support
A price zone where declines have stalled several times, because buyers showed up there. On a buy, the stop loss usually goes below a support. See also the chart patterns.
Swap

The cost (sometimes a small gain) of holding a position overnight, based on the interest rates of the two currencies. At most brokers it is charged triple on Wednesdays, to cover the weekend. See chapter 3.
A style where you hold positions from a few days to a few weeks and work mainly on D1 and H4. It's my style and, for a beginner, a more forgiving one: you have time to think.
Take profit (TP)
The order that automatically closes your position in profit, at the target you set. It goes in a logical place, just before a zone where price may turn around. See chapter 5.
Timeframe
The time period of one candle: M15 (15 minutes), H1 (one hour), H4 (4 hours), D1 (one day), W1 (one week). Small timeframes have a lot of noise. See chapter 2.
Trailing stop
A stop loss that follows the price at a fixed distance when the trade moves in your favour and never moves back. Careful: in MetaTrader it only works while the platform is open.
Trend
The general direction of price over a period: up (higher highs and higher lows), down (lower highs and lows) or sideways. You see it most clearly on the higher timeframes, D1 and H4.
Pip value
How much you win or lose on a 1-pip move. On EURUSD, 1 pip on 1 lot is worth 10 USD; on other pairs it depends on the exchange rate. See the examples in chapter 3.
Base currency and quote currency
In a pair, the first currency is the base and the second is the quote. EURUSD = 1.1000 means 1 euro (the base) costs 1.10 dollars (the quote). See chapter 1.
Volatility
How much and how fast the price moves. Volatility rises around news and during active sessions. A stop loss that's too tight in a volatile market gets hit often.
